text:
Beside Vinca, a little sister, much like her, opened blue eyes in a round, sun-baked face beneath fair hair like stiff stubble, and rested the closed fists of a well-brought-up child on the tablecloth beside her plate. Two identical white dresses clothed the older and the younger girl, ironed, starched, of flounced organdy.

“A Sunday in Tahiti,” Philippe mocked inwardly, “I have never seen her look so ugly.”

Vinca’s mother, Vinca’s father, Vinca’s aunt, Phil and his parents, and the Parisian passing through encircled the table in green sweaters, striped blazers, and tussore jackets. The villa, rented every year by the two families of friends, smelled that morning of hot brioche and floor wax. The graying man, who had come from Paris, represented, among these brightly clad bathers and darkened children, the delicate, pale, well-dressed stranger.

“How you are changing, little Vinca!” he said to the girl.

“Tell me about it,” Phil muttered sourly.

The stranger leaned toward Vinca’s mother to confess to her in a low voice:

“She is becoming ravishing! Ravishing! In two years... you will see!”

Vinca heard, cast a quick feminine glance at the stranger, and smiled. Her crimson mouth parted over a blade of white teeth, her pupils, blue as the flower whose name she bore, were veiled by fair lashes, and Phil himself was dazzled. “Hey!... what has got into her?”

In the canvas-lined hall, Vinca served the coffee. She moved stiffly and without mishap, with a kind of acrobatic charm. When a gust of wind jostled the fragile table, Vinca caught an overturned chair with her foot and, with her chin, a lace mat that was flying away, and at the same time did not cease pouring a flawless stream of coffee into a cup.

“Look at her!” the stranger exclaimed rapturously.

He called her a “Tanagra,” made her taste some Chartreuse, asked her the names of the lovers she was driving to despair at the Cancale casino...

“Ha! Ha! The Cancale casino! But there is no casino in Cancale!”

She laughed, showing the solid semicircle of all her teeth, pivoting like a ballerina on the tips of her white shoes. Cunning was coming to her along with coquetry; she did not turn her gaze toward Philippe, who, gloomy behind the piano and the large bouquet of thistles planted in a copper bucket, was contemplating her.

“I was mistaken,” he admitted to himself. “She is very pretty. That is something new!”

As the stranger, to the sound of the phonograph, proposed teaching Vinca the _balancello_, Philippe slipped outside, ran toward the beach, and curled into a ball in a hollow in the dunes, where he put his head on his arms and his arms on his knees. A new Vinca, full of voluptuous insolence, persisted beneath his closed eyelids: Vinca coquettish, well armed, suddenly augmented by rounded flesh, Vinca wicked and as rebellious as one could wish...

“Phil! My Phil! I was looking for you... What is the matter?”

The seductress, breathless, was beside him, innocently pulling his hair by the handful to make him raise his head.

“There is nothing wrong with me,” he said hoarsely.

He opened his eyes fearfully. Kneeling in the sand, she was crumpling her ten organdy flounces and crawling like a squaw.

“Phil! Please, don’t be angry... You have something against me... Phil, you know very well that I love you more than anyone in the world. Speak to me, Phil!”

He searched her for the fleeting splendor that had irritated him. But now she was nothing more than a dismayed Vinca, an adolescent burdened too soon with the humility, the awkwardness, the dreary obstinacy of true love... He snatched his hand away from her as she kissed it:

“Leave me alone! You don’t understand, you never understand anything!... Get up, come on!”

And as he smoothed the crumpled dress, tied the sash at her waist, and calmed the stiff hair standing up in the wind, he sought to mold upon her once more the shape of the little idol he had glimpsed...




III


“The holidays, now, amount to a month and a half, that’s all!...”

“One month,” said Vinca. “You know very well that I shall be in Paris on September twentieth.”

“Why? Your father is free until October first every year.”

“Yes, but Mother and I, and Lisette, do not have too much time from September twentieth to October fourth for the autumn shopping—a dress for me to wear to class, a coat, a hat, and the same things for Lisette... I meant us, women, after all...”

Phil, lying on his back, tossed handfuls of sand into the air.

“Oh, honestly... ‘You women...’ What a fuss you make over all that!”

“It has to be done... You find your suit laid out on your bed. You concern yourself only with your shoes, because you buy them from a shop your father forbids you to go to; the rest takes care of itself. It is very convenient for you men!...”

Philippe sat up with a jerk of his loins, ready to answer the irony. But Vinca was not making fun of him. She was sewing, edging with pink scallops a crêpon dress the same blue as her eyes. Her fair hair, cut in the Joan of Arc style, was slowly growing longer. Sometimes she parted it at the nape and tied with blue ribbons two short wheat-colored brooms, one along each cheek. Since lunch she had lost one of her ribbons, and half her hair beat against half her face like a spread curtain.

Philippe frowned:

“God, how badly combed your hair is, Vinca!”

She blushed beneath her holiday tan and cast him a humble glance as she pushed her hair behind her ear:

“I know... my hair will look bad as long as it is too short. This hairstyle is just for the meantime...”

“You don’t care about temporary ugliness...” he said harshly.

“I swear I do, Phil.”

Ashamed of so much gentleness, he fell silent, and she raised astonished eyes to him, for she had not expected any leniency. He himself believed this was a temporary truce in his little companion’s touchiness and prepared himself for reproaches, childish sarcasms, for what he called her “greyhound temper.” But she smiled melancholyly, with a wandering smile addressed to the calm sea, to the sky where the high wind traced ferns of cloud.

“On the contrary, I very much want to be pretty, I assure you. Mother says I can still become pretty, but that I must be patient.”

Her proud and awkward fifteen years, trained by running, salted, hardened, thin and sturdy, often made her resemble a stinging, brittle riding switch, but her eyes of incomparable blue and her simple, healthy mouth were finished works of feminine grace.
